articles.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
articles.dek: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach…
paragraphs: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

But bleach can't conquer per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—commonly called PFAS—a class of synthetic chemicals. Resistant to grease and water, they gave us nonstick cookware, waterproofing technology, durable medical devices and firefighting foam. But these substances' ironclad chemical bonds, which earned them the nickname "forever chemicals," have a darker side linked to deadly cancers, infertility, and immune and developmental damage to infants and children.
They might also be called "everywhere chemicals" because they are widely found in basic items like clothes, cosmetics and pizza boxes, as well as soil, air and drinking water.

"PFAS—this guy doesn't care about anything," said Ashburton plant manager Mohammed Almafrachi, Ph. D. '26, as he led the UMD students through the facility last Tuesday. "We can add whatever chemicals we want to the water, but he's going to stay here."

Not if Guangbin Li, UMD assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering, has anything to say about it. Although one government study detected PFAS chemicals in nearly half of the nation's tap water , the PFAS expert envisions a day when the stubborn chemicals can be curbed to the point of eliminating health risks.

For the past two years, he and his students have collaborated with Baltimore's Department of Public Works, which oversees the city's water system, to study PFAS interventions; city officials have provided water samples and data to Li's team, while he has shared his technology with water engineers.
"People call it forever chemicals, but scientifically it's not forever," Li said. "We still have a ways to go, but we have the technology to destroy them."

While many scientists have attempted to lower PFAS by converting it with aggressive heat or electricity to carbon dioxide—nontoxic, but still a gas that contributes to climate change—Li's method uses micrometer-sized adsorbents like carbon that soak the PFAS up like a sponge and lock it in place. The resulting solids either remain safely buried in soil for years or can be removed from treated water after a few hours to a few days.

By experimenting with different chemical combinations with which to arm the adsorbents, Li's aim is to build a kind of super sponge that ensnares not one but the majority of the most dangerous PFAS and converts them into recyclable materials.

At the same time, his research has led him to question the promises of other scientists using similar methods. While some claim that current soil-based adsorbents can trap certain PFAS for up to 100 years, Li has found that the true number could be less than 20 years.
"We should be prepared for a future of these chemicals coming back to us sooner than we think," said Li, who recently published his findings in Environmental Science & Technology .

The Ashburton plant, a large, labyrinthine building erected in 1956, processes up to 165 million gallons (625 million liters) of drinking water a day for consumers stretching from Towson to Columbia, Maryland, but it was never designed to treat PFAS. Li is working with Almafrachi—his former student who runs the Ashburton facility as well as the city's other two filtration plants—to identify opportunities for modifications and pilot programs introducing new adsorbents.

"He has all the scientific and engineering knowledge of PFAS, and we have the operational knowledge," said Almafrachi, who as a UMD doctoral student designed a chemical catalyst that adsorbs PFAS. He calls the collaboration between the university and his team "Terps helping Terps."

Meanwhile, through his connections to Almafrachi and other Baltimore engineers, Li appreciates the chance to expose his students to the real-world infrastructure challenges facing the city, which houses one of the nation's oldest filtration systems.

articles.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years

Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

That's according to new research on a species of fish called blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) recently published in Communications Biology . The study was co-led by Alec Lackmann, Ph. D. , a fisheries research scientist from the Swenson College of Science and Engineering at the University of Minnesota Duluth (UMD), Luke Holmquist, a Missouri River fisheries biologist with Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews, Ph. D. , a fisheries biologist with the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa.

Native to 23 states, including Minnesota and Montana, the blue sucker is categorized as imperiled in 22 of them. Population data over three decades from Montana have shown virtually no small (young) blue suckers coming into the population, suggesting recruitment failure possibly due to habitat fragmentation caused by large dams.

"For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range," said the researchers. "Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap." Those researchers wanted to find out more about the species by examining the age structure, recruitment trends and longevity using recently refined aging techniques.

From 2023 to 2026, the team thoughtfully collected and processed samples of close to 50 fish from a population in Montana to learn more. What they found is completely rewriting our understanding of the species and adds to a growing group of fish that were previously underappreciated but have lifespans often greater than those of human beings.
To precisely age the fish, scientists extract what are called the otoliths, or earstones, from inside the cranium of the fish and then thinly section the stones to determine their age.

Approximately 97% of fish species have otoliths. They're tiny, stone-like structures that grow throughout the fish's lifetime, forming a new layer each year. When processed properly, scientists can examine the otolith with a compound microscope and count the layers, like the rings on a tree, and learn the age of the fish. When Lackmann and his partners found the data from the otoliths to far exceed previous estimates, they then set out to test the validity of the otolith ages.

Lackmann, an expert and pioneer in otolith aging and validation techniques, started on the project in 2023, after fisheries colleagues in Montana had noticed long-term trends that suggested there weren't many new generations of the fish. "Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them," Lackmann said.

In these otoliths from fish previously thought to live to about 40 years, "we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old," he said. "When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity."

To confirm what they were seeing in the microscope was accurate, they used bomb radiocarbon dating, testing the otolith ages both within and across individuals against the known increase in atmospheric radiocarbon levels that came from the widespread nuclear bomb testing in the mid-20th century.

"Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid- to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere," said Lackmann. "This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you're able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc. ) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate.

articles.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
articles.dek: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years.
paragraphs: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation.

"Because we were studying already damaged reefs (in the modern-day Caribbean), we had a limited baseline of what a healthy reef used to look like and were missing understandings of things like resilience," said Claire Williams, who led research on the fossil and modern reefs while earning a doctorate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences. "So, my theory was that by bringing in the fossil record, we could get a richer picture of coral tolerances and make better predictions for the future."

The findings were recently published in Palaios and Conservation Biology . At two sites in Jamaica, the team analyzed the corals found in fossil reefs dating from 125,000 to 130,000 years ago—the Late Pleistocene epoch—a time known for interglacial warming periods. According to Williams, these past warming periods are good analogs for what the planet is projected to experience in about 50 to 100 years.

The fossil reefs are now above sea level, so the researchers adapted a transect method used to monitor modern corals: Instead of swimming above the reefs, the researchers walked along them, photographing the fossils to estimate the number and distribution of corals in an area. They then compared this data from fossil reefs with coral species at modern sites.

At the modern sites, the researchers found that certain branching corals called Acropora—including Acropora palmata and Acropora cervicornis—which were abundant during the Pleistocene, are now largely dead and covered by algae. What's more, most remaining corals are Porites astreoides, a globular species that Williams said can recover quickly after disturbances but doesn't provide helpful reef structure.
"These big branching species provide a lot of habitat and offshore protection. With that gone, we've lost that function on the reef," Williams said.

The solution to rebuilding the reef isn't as simple as planting more Acropora corals in degraded reef environments, said co-author Rowan Martindale, an associate professor at the Jackson School's Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.

"We can nurture and transplant new, healthy corals from nurseries to damaged reefs, often referred to as coral gardening , but if they are in a place that's too hot in the future, they're not going to survive," Martindale said. "Many of the Alligator Head Foundation's transplanted corals died off during the heat-induced bleaching event in the summer of 2023." (The Alligator Head Foundation is a marine conservation group in East Portland, Jamaica. )

With that in mind, the researchers also conducted a study on the ecological niches of ancient corals, analyzing the water temperature and salinity the corals could tolerate. In this analysis, they included data from mid-Holocene fossil records to get data points from a more recent period, 5,000 to 7,000 years ago. This data was then used to predict the places with similar ecological niches to these past environments—helping to indicate where the species might survive in the future.

The researchers also incorporated data from climate models to identify reef areas in the Caribbean that are projected to have the salinity and sea-surface temperature best suited for species that can help foster and grow healthy reef ecosystems in the future. The best spots for conservation include parts of the northern Caribbean, the Florida Keys and the Yucatan Peninsula.

However, Williams said that the team's findings should be thought of as a starting point. Environments need to be consistently monitored and assessed for issues that can interfere with coral survival, such as disease, pollution, natural disasters and other environmental issues.

"The fossil record can improve our predictions and provide best-case ideas of where things might be able to survive," Williams said. "Conservation needs to be adaptive and to keep learning new information."

articles.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
articles.dek: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely…
paragraphs: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.
Now, new research led by Rice University is challenging that assumption.

At a site in the Texas Panhandle, researchers have uncovered evidence that Indigenous hunters repeatedly used a cliff to harvest bison over a period spanning 3,000 years. The discovery marks only the second scientifically verified bison jump in Texas and offers new insight into the ingenuity, cooperation and hunting traditions of ancient communities.
The research, published in the journal American Antiquity , was led by August "Gus" Costa, adjunct lecturer of anthropology at Rice.

Located in Caprock Canyons State Park, the Nighthawk site provides evidence that ancient communities in the region practiced a hunting technique once thought to be largely confined to the northern Great Plains.

Bison jumping involved maneuvering herds toward cliffs, where the animals would fall to their deaths or become incapacitated. Unlike smaller hunting expeditions, these large-scale operations required extensive planning and cooperation among multiple groups of people.

"Bison jumping is exciting because it's a community activity," Costa said. "Large-scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

Hunters likely worked in specialized teams. Some located herds and guided them toward grazing areas near the cliffs, while others emerged from hiding to direct the animals toward the drop. Additional groups dispatched injured bison and processed the meat, hides and other materials.
Costa said these hunts likely served a larger social purpose, bringing communities together for ceremonies, trade and celebrations and to strengthen relationships.

Researchers initially believed the Nighthawk site contained evidence of at least two hunting events based on the stone spear and arrow points discovered there. But further investigation revealed a much longer and more complex history.

Using radiocarbon dating of bison bones, researchers identified evidence of at least seven separate hunting events spanning approximately 3,000 years. The findings suggest generations of hunters returned to the same location despite significant cultural and environmental changes.
Those changes included the transition from stone-tipped spears to bows and arrows, the introduction of pottery and shifts in the surrounding landscape.
Erosion dramatically altered the site over time, moving the cliff's jump-off point approximately the length of a football field. Yet hunters continued returning.
"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," Costa said.

articles.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
articles.dek: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together.
paragraphs: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).

Compared with ordinary excitons, IEs have lifetimes that are tens of times longer and can be more easily controlled by external voltage, making them a key building block for next-generation ultra-low-power optoelectronic devices and quantum computing technologies.

However, conventional 2D semiconductors have had practical limitations: Due to their isotropic structural characteristics, IEs could emit light only at specific angles, such as 0° and 60°, and without polarization.

A research team led by Prof. Jeongyong Kim of the Department of Energy Science has developed, for the first time, a core technology that enables the full control of both the wavelength and polarization of infrared light by simply stacking and twisting two atomically thin semiconductor layers. The achievement was published in ACS Nano .
The team focused on the anisotropic semiconductor materials rhenium disulfide (ReS₂) and rhenium diselenide (ReSe₂), whose optical properties vary depending on crystal orientation.

By stacking two semiconductor layers and precisely twisting them at angles ranging from 1° to 88°, the team created a new moiré pattern between the atomic lattices, similar to the wavelike pattern formed when two mesh screens overlap. Using this moiré structure, the researchers successfully generated stable IE emission in the infrared region at virtually any twist angle.

Furthermore, by precisely tuning both the twist angle and the number of stacked layers, the team achieved a broad energy tuning range of approximately 100 meV. This means that subtle differences in the wavelength of infrared light can be controlled at will, representing a world-leading result that far surpasses previous records in 2D semiconductor research.

The researchers also showed that when multiple layers were stacked, the brightness of the emitted light increased up to an order of magnitude, and the polarization direction of the light could also be controlled. In other words, they established a new technology platform capable of simultaneously controlling both the color (wavelength) and direction (polarization) of light within a single quantum-scale semiconductor structure.

Kim said, "We have, for the first time in the world, demonstrated a technology that can simultaneously control the wavelength and polarization of infrared light based on interlayer excitons simply by twisting atomically thin semiconductor layers."

He added, "By overcoming the limitations of existing 2D materials, this technology establishes a new materials platform for polarization-addressable infrared emitters and angle-sensitive photodetectors, and is expected to contribute to advanced applications including lidar sensors for autonomous vehicles, night-vision imaging, and biosensors."

articles.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
articles.dek: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical…
paragraphs: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems .

The researchers surveyed almost 400 Gen Z consumers in India. Structural equation modeling, a statistical method for examining relationships between different factors, was used to analyze the survey results. They found that gamification, which involves incorporating game-like elements such as rewards and interactive tasks into nongaming applications, was a strong predictor of willingness to use mobile payments.

Moreover, a positive attitude toward the technology, encouragement from peers and confidence in using it all increased engagement with gamified features. That engagement, in turn, strongly predicted intentions to adopt mobile payments.

The work draws on social learning theory to help explain how people acquire behavior by observing others, as well as the theory of planned behavior, which links attitudes, social expectations and perceived control to individual decisions.

The findings could be useful in promoting financial inclusion in developing economies, where women continue to face structural barriers to economic participation. The researchers suggest that expanding digital infrastructure and making payment platforms more accessible could help bring underserved groups into formal financial systems. For fintech (financial technology) companies, the results also indicate that reward-based interfaces can be designed for broad audiences without requiring gender-specific approaches to user engagement.

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
articles.dek: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.
paragraphs: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U. S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U. S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1. 3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.
Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc. , selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.
Complete lists of the selected proposals are available on the SBIR/STTR program’s website:
NASA’s SBIR/STTR program is part of the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate and is managed by NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find New Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults
articles.dek: Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.
paragraphs: Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology , researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph. D. , a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.
The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M. D. , Ph. D. , a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions.”

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr. , M. D. , a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

articles.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
articles.dek: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .
paragraphs: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.
“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.
My sister was one of 43. 5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

articles.title: Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds
articles.dek: A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.
paragraphs: A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz , examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.
Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.
During angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93. 3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

articles.title: NASA Honor Awards Ceremony Recognizes Employees at Stennis Space Center
articles.dek: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.
paragraphs: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.

Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return humans to the Moon.

Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing NASA Stennis propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs.

Bradley Tyree of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Engineering Excellence Award for engineering excellence and contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program.

Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for exceptional environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships, streamlined agency processes, and reduced regulatory risk.

Daniel Jones of Huntsville, Alabama, received the Excellence in Innovation Award for the invention of the Hydrocarbon Propellants Enabling Reproduction of Flows in Rocket Engines, a system for low-cost aerodynamic data acquisition.

Peyton Pinson of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Leadership Excellence Award for exceptional leadership as E-1 test director, providing steady guidance and strengthening team cohesion throughout a demanding and high-tempo year of propulsion testing.

Joseph Schuyler of Pass Christian, Mississippi, received the J. Harry Guin Leadership Award for transformative leadership that advanced NASA Stennis propulsion testing capability and strengthened its role as the agency’s Center of Excellence in Propulsion Testing.

Michael McDaniel of Slidell, Louisiana, received the Roy S. Estess Service Leadership Award for exceptional partnership, sustained leadership, and an unwavering commitment to his community as the general manager of L3Harris Technologies at NASA Stennis that embodies the legacy of the late center director.

Amer Arshad of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership, system stewardship, and collaborative solutions that have strengthened NASA’s mission through improved reliability, insight, and efficiency.

Claire O’Shaughnessy of Mandeville, Louisiana, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership and collaborative drive that strengthened the center’s mission by advancing critical facility capabilities for the agency’s Artemis program.

In addition to individual awards, the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment, Confined by Missile Test Team received the Space Flight Awareness Team Award for exceptional technical achievement in executing a test series that has provided mission critical safety data for the future of human spaceflight.

Briou Bourgeois accepted the award on behalf of the team, which included: Chase Aubry, Brandon Carver, Jack Conley, James Connell, Armando Delgado, Mateo Ferreira, Pau Fuller, Mark Hancock, Steven Helmstetter, Paula Hensarling, Jason Hopper, Chase Lemaire, Addison Mitchell, Randall Pigott, Stephen Rawls, Skip Roberts, Mark Robinson, Luke Roger, Matthew Sappington, Robert Simmers, Jason Richard, Bradley Tyree, Richard Wear, and Robert Williams.

The ceremony also honored employees who reached significant milestone anniversaries in their civil service careers. Employees with 40 years of service were Curtis Armstrong, Jason Edge, and Kevin Power. Employees with 35 years of service were Michael Brashear, Reginald Ellis II, Arlen Griffey, Bradley Messer, Christine Powell, and Michael Rewis. Skip Roberts was recognized for 30 years of service. Employees with 25 years of service were Gregory Carmouche, Thomas Carroll, Craig Chandler, Jorge Figueroa, Jared Grover, Melissa Huggins, Scott Jensen, Jeffrey Lott, Christopher Mulkey, Richard Rauch, Ryan Roberts, Karen Seals, Joseph Schuyler, Peterve Tran, and Maury Vander.

articles.title: The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal
articles.dek: The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.
paragraphs: The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.

Among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl. Buried alongside her was an exceptionally rare copper neck ring, an object that raises an intriguing question about life thousands of years ago. Was she born into a wealthy family, or did her elaborate burial reflect something else about how her community valued status?
For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.

Developed by University of Copenhagen archaeologist Mikkel Nørtoft during his PhD research, QuantWealth combines multiple forms of archaeological evidence to reconstruct social status, displays of wealth, and inequality. In a study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology , Nørtoft and his colleague Adam B. Rohrlach applied the method to 296 graves belonging to the Corded Ware culture in present-day Bohemia, dating from approximately 2900 to 2300 BCE.

The researchers examined burial practices and grave goods alongside genetic ancestry, Y-chromosome patterns that trace paternal lineages, and skeletal evidence of age, sex, and pathological conditions. By comparing these different clues, they could investigate how social differences changed across several centuries. The findings suggest that inequality developed gradually rather than emerging as a firmly established social hierarchy when migrants from the eastern European steppe settled in the region.

The Corded Ware culture formed part of a much larger transformation in prehistoric Europe, when populations migrating from the steppe helped spread early Indo-European dialects across the continent. Archaeologists have debated whether these newcomers also introduced strongly patriarchal societies in which wealth and power passed primarily through family lines. The evidence from Bohemia points toward a more complicated history.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy. Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually. Achieving status through life-actions appears to have been more important than through inheritance, at least during the first 400 years”, says Nørtoft, the study’s lead author.

During the earliest period, approximately 2900 to 2700 BCE, burial practices suggest that the newly established communities placed considerable emphasis on shared traditions. Differences in grave wealth were relatively small and largely associated with age. There was little evidence of pronounced gender inequality, and power appeared to be distributed among several paternal lineages with steppe ancestry.
Nørtoft connects this early pattern to the circumstances surrounding the migrants’ arrival in Central Europe.

“Following a few harsh years of ‘dark sun’ clouded by a devastating volcanic eruption 2,900 BCE, the earliest herder communities, settling in Bohemia around 2,900-2,700 BCE, seem to have focused mostly on building social cohesion across this new network of migrants in Central Europe. In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Mikkel Nørtoft explains.

Between approximately 2700 and 2500 BCE, however, burial customs began to change. The appearance of a new paternal lineage coincided with increasingly elaborate funerals, including greater concentrations of prestigious objects and meat offerings. Exchange networks expanded, and differences between male and female burials became more pronounced.

Adult men were particularly likely to receive richly furnished graves, while younger adults became increasingly common among those buried. Despite this growing competition for status, the skeletal evidence did not show a clear corresponding increase in injuries associated with violence.

The final phase, spanning roughly 2500 to 2300 BCE, brought further changes. One paternal lineage had become dominant in the burial record, and a small number of children received unusually wealthy burials. Because children had less opportunity to accumulate status through their own accomplishments, these graves raise the possibility that some families had begun passing social advantages between generations.

“In the final phase, roughly 2,500-2,300 BCE, we see a few rich displays of family wealth through children, and the previously new lineage now dominated the burial record. So maybe the new lineage had gained the most followers and power through the competitive burial parties, and their descendants were now competing among themselves,” Mikkel Nørtoft points out and adds:

articles.title: Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory
articles.dek: Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a…
paragraphs: Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

At Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

Why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a new one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.
Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

The researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

That ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.
The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

articles.title: On the Brink of Extinction, These Giant Sea Turtles Are Doing Something Unexpected
articles.dek: A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.
paragraphs: A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.

When a critically endangered leatherback sea turtle named Bella came ashore in Ecuador in January 2026, her search for a nesting spot took an unexpected turn. Confused by nearby streetlights, she climbed over a rock breakwater at Playa de Crucita and ended up on a sidewalk instead of the sandy beach where she needed to lay her eggs.

Bella eventually returned to the ocean without nesting, but two nights later, she tried again on a quieter stretch of beach. This time, she successfully buried 47 eggs in the sand. A few weeks later, 44 baby turtles emerged and made their way toward the sea.

Her persistence is part of a potentially hopeful development for the eastern Pacific leatherback, a critically endangered population of the world’s largest sea turtle. During the 2025–2026 nesting season, researchers documented a record number of leatherback nests along several beaches in Ecuador, more than 1,000 miles from the turtles’ traditional nesting grounds in Mexico and Costa Rica.

The findings raise an intriguing possibility. As ocean temperatures change, some leatherbacks may be adjusting where they reproduce, taking advantage of cooler conditions along Ecuador’s coast. Whether this represents a lasting adaptation remains uncertain, but successful nesting in new locations could offer opportunities for a population that has declined dramatically.

“Historically, observing female Eastern Pacific leatherbacks on Ecuador’s beaches was a rare or unusual event, but our findings suggest they are adapting their reproductive cycle to thrive and survive in coastal Ecuador,” says Juan José Alava, a marine ecotoxicologist, adjunct professor at Simon Fraser University’s School of Resource and Environmental Management, and leading co-author of the study.

In a study published in Chelonian Conservation and Biology , researchers examined more than 45 years of records documenting reproductive-age female turtles, nesting attempts, nests, hatching success, and stranded turtles along Ecuador’s coastline. They compared these observations with El Niño and La Niña events, which bring warmer and cooler ocean conditions.

Over the past decade, the records showed increased leatherback activity and nesting during cooler La Niña periods in the southeastern tropical Pacific. This relationship suggests that ocean temperatures may influence where females lay their eggs, although the findings do not establish that warming waters are directly causing them to move.

The Ecuadorian nests also showed encouraging results. The number of eggs per nest and the proportion that successfully hatched were comparable to those recorded at traditional nesting sites farther north. In some cases, Alava says, Ecuadorian nests produced more hatchlings than usual.

Leatherbacks are particularly well suited to life across dramatically different ocean environments. They are the only sea turtles that thrive in both warm and cold conditions, traveling thousands of miles between tropical nesting beaches and subpolar Pacific feeding grounds, where they feast on jellyfish during the summer. Their extensive travels have even brought them to Canada’s west coast, with more than 150 records from British Columbia waters between 1931 and 2024.

Despite that remarkable flexibility, eastern Pacific leatherbacks have suffered a population decline of more than 90 percent since the 1980s. Their survival is threatened by unusually warm El Niño conditions, which are worsened by human-caused climate change, as well as fishing bycatch, plastic pollution, vessel strikes, egg harvesting, and the loss of nesting habitat.

“It signals new hope for a subspecies of leatherback on track for extinction in the eastern Pacific within 60 years. They are making their way alongside nature against all odds, representing hope for this species and other sea turtle species even as they reach tipping points.”

Bella’s nesting success offers one example of what Ecuador’s beaches could provide. After researchers tagged her during her first unsuccessful attempt, they discovered that she nested four to five times in 2026 alone. One nest was left in its original location, while the others were moved to the San Jacinto hatchery.
Across the season, Bella laid 146 eggs, producing 134 hatchlings for an overall success rate of 91. 8 percent.

articles.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
articles.dek: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral.
paragraphs: A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?
The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.
While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements .

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.
Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U. S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.
However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services .

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born .
The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17. 99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.
When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.
Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage .

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

articles.title: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
articles.dek: The U. S. State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.
paragraphs: The U. S. State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.

The grant, first reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026 , would support research to document the “ hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” experienced by Afrikaners – descendants of white Dutch settlers who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.
As scholars who study foreign aid and civil society organizations , we would see U. S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs the U. S. has funded in the past .
The U. S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and strengthen human rights protections .

Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U. S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy.

Past administrations called this assistance “ fundamental ” to the goals of U. S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost $3 billion annually .

Some of this money has supported NGOs engaged in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where civil society is especially at risk .
NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help stave off future violence .
The Trump administration suspended most U. S. foreign aid in January 2025 , soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.

It then dismantled USAID , the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending . It has continued to take steps in that direction with or without lawmakers’ cooperation .
As a result, many lifesaving public health programs lost funding. This policy change has had an enormous human toll , which public health researchers have begun to quantify .

In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. USAID’s Democracy Fund , which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s funding and staffing for promoting democracy were also slashed .

In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the benefits of these efforts . The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.
By contrast, AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history , without any evident effort to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa.
It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “ white genocide ” in that country.

In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be victims of crime and other forms of violence compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa.
By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the dubious claims the group makes about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.

And the Trump administration’s embrace of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U. S. has allowed thousands of white South Africans to come to the U. S. as refugees while denying admission to nearly all other refugees from the rest of the world.

articles.title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
articles.dek: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.
paragraphs: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor , I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher , I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two .

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism , which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “ aesthetic ” and “ ethical ” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote .

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires , not principles.
Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction : a pattern that we feel compelled to continue , despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction ,” and whether love can become one , but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two .

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.
At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “ a kind of despair ,” rooted in estrangement from oneself , a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.
Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “ Either/Or ” and in “ Works of Love ,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.
Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love .”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote .

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves , a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.
